entry.hook: Puxian Zhenren (a Jin Xian who never once begged for the Dao's mercy) was the most silent blade among the Twelve Golden Immortals. Every time he stepped onto the battlefield, the war ended—not because he was cruel, but because his power arrived already final.

body.body_1:
普贤真人 · True Man of Universal Worthiness / 九宫山白鹤洞普贤真人 (Puxian Zhenren of White Crane Cave, Nine Palaces Mountain)  
Affiliation: 阐教 · 元始天尊门下 · 十二金仙 (The Teaching of Interpretation, disciple of Yuanshi Tianzun, one of the Twelve Golden Immortals)  
Birth Era: Primordial Age (Honghuang Ji Yuan)  
Place of Origin: White Crane Cave, Nine Palaces Mountain  
Current Realm: Fo — Bodhisattva rank in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
body.body_2: At the height of the Feng Shen Da Jie, Puxian Zhenren held the stable celestial rank of Jin Xian (Golden Immortal), a state in which no karmic debt was owed to the Dao. He had never passed through the mortal stages of Qi Refining, Foundation Establishment, or Golden Core formation; his existence was shaped directly from the primordial order. After the war, he accepted the invitation of the Western Teaching and transformed into Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, residing in the Pure Land as the embodiment of great practice. The sources do not record a moment of hesitation or refusal—only a quiet crossing of the threshold.
body.body_3: Puxian Zhenren's entry into the Dao was not a story of sudden enlightenment or mortal desperation. As a direct disciple of Yuanshi Tianzun, his cultivation began in the earliest reaches of the Honghuang Era, before the Great Disconnection. The tradition does not preserve a record of his first breath of Qi or the terror of inner vision hallucinations—likely because he was never a mortal who needed to force the Dao into his body. Instead, his awakening is described as an unfolding: he came into being already aligned with the cosmic order, and his cultivation was a matter of deepening a harmony that had never broken.
body.body_4: The Jin Xian path bypasses the mortal metabolic shutdown and the slow death of human emotion that defines the rogue cultivator's Zhu Ji stage. Puxian Zhenren never experienced the craving for food or the numbness of lost attachment. The tradition presents him as having been born without the parasitic Three Worms; his compassion was never a residue of earthly sentiment but a pure, unshakable resolve. When he later returned to the mortal world during the Feng Shen Da Jie, he moved among humans without the ghost-like distance that haunts the self-made Xian. He felt their suffering—but as a physician feels a pulse, not as a drowning man remembers dry land.
body.body_5: No Jin Dan compresses stolen energy in his dantian; no karmic time bomb ticks in his chest. As a Jin Xian, Puxian Zhenren's power is a direct, low-resistance conduit of the Dao itself. He has never faced the Three Calamities—Thunder, Yin Fire, or Keening Wind—because his presence causes no imbalance in the cosmic ledger. His cultivation owes nothing to the universe, and the universe owes him nothing. In battle, this gives him a terrifying freedom: he is not conserving strength against a future tribulation, because there is no future tribulation to fear.
body.body_6: The excision of the Three Worms—a form of self-execution practiced by mortal Xian—was never required of Puxian Zhenren. The sources do not describe a moment when greed, anger, or lust was cut from his being, because these attachments were never part of his original constitution. There is no second face in his dantian, no Nascent Soul that threatens to replace him. He is not in a war between "who he was" and "who he is becoming"; he has always been a single, stable field of awareness and action.
body.body_7: The central drive of Puxian Zhenren's existence is not fear of death or a hunger for eternal life, but an unwavering commitment to cosmic duty and the alleviation of suffering. The legend frames him as a being of pure compassion and resolute will—he does not waver because there is nothing in him to waver. Yet this very steadiness becomes the axis of his deepest paradox: he could kill a demon in the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation without rage, and later bless that same demon's reincarnation without sentiment. The tradition does not treat this as coldness, but as a higher form of mercy that burns away the personal. Whether he sacrificed something human to reach this state is a question the sources leave open, preferring to honor the result rather than the price.
body.body_8: Within the Chan Jiao (阐教), Puxian Zhenren stood as a trusted executor of Yuanshi Tianzun's will. He fought alongside his fellow Twelve Golden Immortals, never for glory but for the structural integrity of the divine order. His most noted opponent was Lingya Xian (灵牙仙), a powerful demon from the rival Jie Jiao (截教), whom he subdued in the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation with overwhelming force. After that victory, Ran Deng Daoren—acting on Yuanshi Tianzun's secret instruction—guided him and Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun toward the Western Teaching. They accepted the invitation of Amitabha Buddha and Zhunti Daoren, leaving the Xian path permanently. No record exists of conflict with the Shen (god) bureaucracy or the Mo (demon) path; his interactions with mortals were indirect, mediated by the scale of the war.
body.body_9: Today, Puxian Zhenren no longer resides in White Crane Cave, Nine Palaces Mountain, or any domain of the Xian. He has fully transitioned to the Pure Land as Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, where he expounds the *Ten Great Vows* (十大愿王) that guide cultivators of all paths toward the realization of ultimate practice. His former Jin Xian body has been sublated into a Bodhisattva form that retains its original power while taking on additional faculties of compassion and active guidance. He no longer belongs to the Xian path's reckoning—his karmic ledger is now closed within the Buddha-field.
body.body_10: None. The sources do not record a specific physical relic, sword scar, or temple that is uniquely tied to Puxian Zhenren's Xian identity. His legacy is carried forward through the *Avatamsaka Sutra* and the *Vows of Samantabhadra*, texts of doctrine rather than stone or bronze.
body.body_11: This entry is closely linked to the other members of the Twelve Golden Immortals, particularly Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun, who shared the same conversion path to the Western Teaching. The master-discipline relationship with Yuanshi Tianzun forms the root of his Chan Jiao identity. Ran Deng Daoren and Zhunti Daoren appear as the immediate agents of his conversion. His sole recorded battle victory over Lingya Xian places him in connection with the Jie Jiao lineage and the broader Feng Shen Da Jie conflict.

guide.guide_1: Imagine a man who walks into a room, and the room falls silent. Not because he is loud or angry, but because everyone already knows the argument is over. That was Puxian Zhenren. He was the quietest of the Twelve Golden Immortals—the one who barely spoke, who never bragged, who appeared only at the moment when a battle had to be finished. And when he did, it was finished. No speeches. No second chances. Just a calm, heavy finality that made you wonder: was that never a fight, or was he just that far ahead of everyone else?
guide.guide_2: You may have heard of him differently—as Pu Xian Pu Sa, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the one who rides a six-tusked white elephant and represents the great practice of the Buddha's path. That's the later version. But before he was a Bodhisattva, he was a Golden Immortal: a Xian who never stole anything from the Dao, who never owed a karmic debt, who didn't have to run from Tian Jie. He was one of the Twelve Golden Immortals of Chan Jiao, the elite disciples of Yuanshi Tianzun. The tradition usually skips over his Xian years and jumps straight to the Buddhist part. But his Xian self is worth knowing, because it is the strangest kind of power: power without guilt.
guide.guide_3: How do you become a Golden Immortal if you never had to crawl through the mud of mortal cultivation? The answer is: you don't become one. You are born one. Puxian Zhenren was not a human who clawed his way up. He was a direct emanation of the Dao, shaped by Yuanshi Tianzun in the primordial deep time. He never knew the terror of first Qi absorption, never felt his gut contract during Bi Gu, never saw a Nascent Soul stare back at him with a stranger's face. The price he paid was not the price of the rogue Xian—the loss of taste, tears, or memory. The price he paid was simply that he never had a self to lose. He was a function of the cosmos from the beginning. If you think that's a blessing, ask yourself: would you trade your entire childhood for a perfect engine?
guide.guide_4: Let's try Puxian's version of the Xian cost ledger. Mortal Xian lose food, love, fear, sleep, and finally their own face. What does a Jin Xian lose? Nothing, because there is nothing to lose—and that is the cost. He does not experience the ache of homesickness on a rainy night. He does not know the full-body heat of unexpected joy. When he looks at an old friend, he sees the friend's karmic function, not the shared laughter of a thousand years ago. The tradition calls this "stillness" and admires it. But think of it: a perfect instrument, forever tuned, forever playing the right note, and never once moved by the music. That is Puxian Zhenren's version of immortality. It is cleaner than the blood-soaked path of the rogue Xian—but it is also emptier, like a bell that rings on command but has never chosen to sing.
guide.guide_5: Why did he keep walking? If you are already a perfect instrument of the Dao, why accept the invitation of the Western Teaching and become a Bodhisattva? The tradition does not give him a tortured motive—no mid-life crisis, no hidden wound. The answer is simpler and weirder: he was needed. The Feng Shen Da Jie reshuffled the cosmic order, and the Western Teaching needed someone who could embody pure, active compassion without the emotional tremors that would compromise a mortal convert. Puxian was the obvious choice. He switched paths not because he was broken, but because he was useful. Read that sentence again. Then ask yourself: would you trade everything you are—your anger, your love, your little messes—for the kind of perfect utility that makes you the most useful being in the universe?
guide.guide_6: The most human moment in Puxian Zhenren's entire record is also the least: he fought Lingya Xian in the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation, subdued him, and then—according to some versions—let him live. Not out of mercy that felt like a decision, but out of a calm recognition that the demon was not evil, simply misplaced. He could do that because he had no personal grudge. And that is exactly why he could never have a real friendship. His relationship with Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun is described as "cooperative" in the sources, not "close." They served the same master, shared the same conversion, now sit in the same Buddha-field. But did they drink tea together? Did they ever share a silence that felt like understanding? We will never know, because the sources do not bother with such questions. That is the loneliness of the Jin Xian: everyone respects you, but no one asks if you are lonely, because they already know the answer is irrelevant.
guide.guide_7: So where does that leave us? Puxian Zhenren is not a tragedy in the way of the rogue Xian—he didn't lose his face, his tears, his humanity. He never had them. Which is more disturbing? The man who sacrifices his soul for immortality and ends up hollow, or the man who was born hollow and never knew there was anything to lose? His story reaches across the gap between the Xian and the Buddha paths, and at its heart sits a question that belongs to everyone: If you could become perfect—perfectly useful, perfectly calm, perfectly right—would you take the deal, knowing that the price is never again feeling wrong? Puxian Zhenren took that deal, and the universe became a slightly better place for it. But the deal also made him the loneliest being in the cosmos, because perfect emptiness is the only thing that cannot miss company. Think about that the next time you are grateful for your terrible, beautiful, imperfect heart.

seo.meta_description: Puxian Zhenren: one of the Twelve Golden Immortals of Chan Jiao, so stable he owed no karmic debt. Later became Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Discover the cost of perfect stillness.
seo.og_title: Puxian Zhenren: The Xian Who Never Owed the Dao a Single Coin
seo.og_description: He was the quietest of the Twelve Golden Immortals, and the most dangerous. No tribulation, no karmic debt, no lost humanity—because he never had humanity to lose. Read his full profile.
seo.twitter_title: Puxian Zhenren: Golden Immortal, Later Bodhisattva
seo.twitter_description: The only Xian who never stole from the Dao. Later became Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. His power was final, and his price was emptiness.

lore_entries.description: The secluded cave dwelling of Puxian Zhenren on Nine Palaces Mountain (九宫山), used before the Feng Shen Da Jie.
The mountain that served as Puxian Zhenren's Xian home, location of White Crane Cave.
A demon-cultivator from the rival Jie Jiao, subdued by Puxian Zhenren during the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation battle; later taken as a mount.
The final large-scale formation battle of the Feng Shen Da Jie, where the Chan Jiao and Western Teaching fought the Jie Jiao.
A senior figure within Chan Jiao who guided Puxian Zhenren and Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun toward the Western Teaching on Yuanshi Tianzun's secret instruction.
One of the two founding saints of the Western Teaching (Jie Yin and Zhunti), who personally received Puxian Zhenren's conversion.
The Buddha presiding over the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; with Zhunti Daoren, he received Puxian Zhenren into the Western Teaching.
The ten vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva that define the practice of active compassion and service in the Huayan school of Buddhism.
A major Mahayana sutra that features Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as a central figure; widely referenced in later Buddhist tradition.

faq_entries.question: Was Puxian Zhenren always a Xian before becoming a Bodhisattva?
faq_entries.answer: Yes. He was one of the Twelve Golden Immortals under Yuanshi Tianzun in the Chan Jiao before he converted to the Western Teaching after the Feng Shen Da Jie.

faq_entries.question: Did Puxian Zhenren experience the Three Calamities (San Zai)?
faq_entries.answer: No. As a Jin Xian (Golden Immortal), he incurred no karmic debt from cultivation and therefore never triggered the Dao's self-correction mechanism.

faq_entries.question: What is his most famous combat feat?
faq_entries.answer: He single-handedly subdued Lingya Xian, a powerful demon from the Jie Jiao, during the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation battle.

faq_entries.question: Why did he leave the Xian path and become a Bodhisattva?
faq_entries.answer: The tradition records that Yuanshi Tianzun secretly instructed Ran Deng Daoren to guide him and Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun toward the Western Teaching as part of the cosmic restructuring.

faq_entries.question: Does he have a specific magical artifact?
faq_entries.answer: The primary sources do not specify a named artifact unique to Puxian Zhenren. His power is described as intrinsic rather than weapon-based.

relation_entries.relation_type: fellow Golden Immortal / same conversion path
